clues.clue: Bakery legend links this flaky crescent to Vienna, but France turned it into the standard breakfast pastry.
Fried eggs on warm tortillas under a chunky tomato salsa make this Mexican breakfast, 'ranch style'.
Tunisia and Israel share this breakfast of eggs poached right in a skillet of spiced tomatoes and peppers.
Chinese breakfast tables ladle out this soupy rice porridge, topped with pickles, peanuts or pork floss.
Sticky, stringy and pungent, this dish of fermented soybeans is the Japanese breakfast that dares a visitor.
A French chef's classic test of skill is this folded egg dish, ideally pale gold and never browned.
A poached egg and Canadian bacon ride an English muffin under a blanket of hollandaise in this brunch order.
Baked or broiled flat instead of folded, this Italian egg dish takes its name from the word for 'fried'.
London's Fortnum & Mason claims it created this picnic staple: a boiled egg wrapped in sausage, crumbed and fried.
Cured for weeks in ash, salt and lime, this Chinese delicacy turns the white amber and the yolk dark green.
Pat's and Geno's glare at each other across a South Philadelphia corner, both selling this sliced-ribeye sandwich.
Ham, roast pork, Swiss and pickles get pressed flat between crusty bread in this specialty of Tampa and Miami.
Corned beef, sauerkraut and Russian dressing meet melted Swiss on grilled rye in this deli order.
Ham and Gruyere bake under bechamel in this Paris cafe staple; add a fried egg and it becomes a 'madame'.
A New Orleans grocery claims it built the first of these round Sicilian loaves stuffed with cold cuts and olive salad.
Three slices of toast, turkey, bacon and tomato stack up in this double-decker with a four-letter, members-only name.
This towering everything-in-the-icebox sandwich is named for the always-hungry husband in the comic strip 'Blondie'.
Dipped in batter, griddled and dusted with powdered sugar, this ham-and-cheese sandwich shares a name with a Dumas count.
Philippe's and Cole's, two old Los Angeles institutions, each claim they invented this roast beef sandwich served with jus.
A 1929 New Orleans streetcar strike gave this sandwich its name after a shop fed the strikers for free.
Traditionally made from water buffalo milk, this soft white cheese melts across a Neapolitan pizza.
This English cheese is named for the Somerset gorge and village where it was once aged in caves.
This Dutch cheese took the name of the market town where it was weighed and sold, not where it was made.
A high melting point lets this Cypriot cheese hit the grill and come off with stripes instead of puddles.
Protected-origin rules bar this English blue cheese from being made in the Cambridgeshire village it is named for.
Four wafer fingers snap apart in this bar from York, England, whose slogan urges you to take a break.
A row of triangular peaks said to echo the Matterhorn gives this Swiss chocolate bar its unmistakable shape.
Carbon dioxide sealed under pressure makes this candy crackle and fizz the instant it hits your tongue.
Leo Hirschfield named this chewy penny candy of 1896 for his young daughter's nickname.
Rodolphe Lindt's 1879 machine smooths gritty chocolate for hours; the process is named for its shell-shaped trough.
Hungarian cooks stir this red powder of dried ground peppers into goulash by the spoonful.
Each purple crocus yields just three crimson threads of this, the priciest spice by weight.
Americans call the fresh leaf cilantro; the dried seed of the very same plant is sold under this name.
The lacy red webbing wrapped around a nutmeg seed is dried and sold as this separate spice.
Not a true pepper at all, this Chinese spice numbs and tingles the lips in fiery 'mala' cooking.
Beets turn this Eastern European soup deep red; a spoonful of sour cream swirls it pink.
Andalusia beats the summer heat with this chilled soup of tomatoes, cucumber, bread and olive oil.
Star anise and charred ginger perfume the beef broth of this Vietnamese noodle soup.
Marseille fishermen turned the part of the catch they could not sell into this saffron-scented seafood soup.
British officers in India carried home this soup whose name comes from Tamil words for 'pepper water'.
A dark roux plus okra or file powder thickens this Louisiana pot, ladled over rice.
This Burgundian braise of beef in red wine gets bacon, pearl onions and mushrooms folded in near the end.
Black beans and salted pork simmer into this Brazilian national dish, served with rice and orange slices.
Named for the earthenware pot it bakes in, this dish of Languedoc layers white beans, sausage and duck confit.
Sumatran cooks simmer beef in coconut milk and spices for hours, until the sauce disappears into this dry dish.
In India, tea boiled up with milk, sugar and cardamom goes by this name, a word that simply means 'tea'.
A bamboo whisk froths this powdered green tea into the centerpiece of the Japanese tea ceremony.
Partly oxidized, this Chinese tea sits between green and black, and its name means 'black dragon'.
Russian tea culture centers on this metal urn, which keeps water hot under a small pot of strong concentrate.
Beans that have passed through this Indonesian tree-climbing mammal become kopi luwak, a famously pricey brew.
Deep-dish pizza and Italian beef sandwiches are hometown specialties of this Midwestern city.
This New England state named the whoopie pie its official treat and the blueberry pie its official dessert.
Diners in this Southwestern state ask 'Red or green?', and the answer decides which chile sauce you get.
Rival bars in this Minnesota city both claim the Juicy Lucy, a burger with the cheese sealed inside the patty.
In 1926 a hotel chef in this Kentucky city invented the Hot Brown, open-faced turkey under bubbling Mornay sauce.
Southern breakfast plates pile this creamy ground-corn dish beside eggs, or under shrimp in the Lowcountry.
The Anchor Bar says that in 1964 its cook deep-fried these, doused them in hot sauce and named them for her New York city.
Ordered 'three-way', this Ohio city's cinnamon-scented meat sauce arrives over spaghetti under shredded cheddar.
Black-eyed peas and rice make this dish with a man's name, eaten on New Year's Day for luck in the South.
Hawaii's plate-lunch classic tops a scoop of rice with a hamburger patty, a fried egg and brown gravy.
